newsitem.title: USA: U.S. urges quick moves to back Brcko decision.
newsitem.headline: U.S. urges quick moves to back Brcko decision.

text.p: The United States on Thursday stressed the need for quick international action to support a controversial decision on the fate of the strategic Bosnian town of Brcko due to be announced on Friday.

Some U.S. officials fear the issue of who will be given control of Brcko is so explosive that fighting will break out no matter what the decision is and the whole U.S.-mediated Bosnia peace agreement could unravel.
State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns refused to comment on what conclusion Roberts Owens, an American arbitrator handling the Brcko case, had arrived at.
Owens is to announce his decision in Rome after a meeting with the Contact Group on former Yugoslavia and the world community's high representative for Bosnia, Carl Bildt.

Brcko, which lies on the Sava River, sits on a narrow land corridor which links eastern and western halves of Serb-controlled territory in northern Bosnia and was seized by the Bosnian Serbs early in the 1992-95 war.
The dispute over who should control it almost caused peace talks in Dayton, Ohio which ended the conflict to collapse in November 1995.
Burns said "we (the United States) believe the international community must move quickly to provide support for the implementation of the Brcko solution once it's announced."
"It's a very emotional issue ... We think it's one that has to be handled quite sensitively," he told reporters.
But he insisted "I don't want to assume the worst is going to happen" and war will re-ignite.
The 1995 U.S.-mediated Dayton peace accords "have turned the situation around for the better, and we expect that that trend will continue," Burns said.
In Rome, a diplomatic source quoted by Reuters said Owens would award Brcko to the Serbs subject to certain guarantees.

The source, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said he expected the Contact Group, comprising Britain, France, Germany, Italy, Russia, the United States and the European Union presidency, to support the ruling.
But the Washington Post reported on Thursday that Owens has decided to place the town under international supervision for a year during which refugees would be helped to resettle in the area.
The newspaper said the decision likely was to be coupled with the announcement of a beefed-up international police presence in Brcko to provide security for returning refugees.
But Burns said the decision to be announced by Owens "will not require us to deploy additional troops to Bosnia."
